questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Define the following terms:

(i) Demand-pull inflation.

(ii) Cost-push inflation.

(iii) Supply of money.

(iv) Demand for money.

(4 x 2 = 8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Demand-pull inflation.** A sustained rise in the general level of prices caused by **aggregate demand growing faster than aggregate supply**, so that too much money chases too few goods. It is typical when the economy is near full employment, or when the government or banks increase the money supply sharply.

2. **Cost-push inflation.** A sustained rise in the general level of prices caused by an **increase in the costs of production** (wages, raw materials, imported inputs, fuel, taxes), which firms pass on to consumers in higher prices, even though demand has not increased.

3. **Supply of money.** The **total amount of money available in the economy** at a given time, made up of the currency (notes and coins) in circulation plus the bank deposits that can be used for payments.

4. **Demand for money.** The **desire of people and firms to hold their wealth in the form of cash** (liquid form) rather than in other assets. It arises from the **transactions motive** (to buy goods and services), the **precautionary motive** (for emergencies) and the **speculative motive** (to take advantage of changes in interest rates or prices); it is also called liquidity preference.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Explain how the Central Bank of your country can regulate the supply of money in the economy.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Central Bank is the bank of the government and of the commercial banks and is responsible for **monetary policy**. For Cameroon, this role is played by the regional central bank of the CEMAC zone. It controls the supply of money mainly by influencing the **amount of credit** that commercial banks can create. If the economy suffers from inflation, it applies a **tight (contractionary) policy**; if there is unemployment and slack demand, it applies an **easy (expansionary) policy**. The main instruments are as follows.

1. **Open market operations.** The Central Bank buys and sells government securities (treasury bills and bonds) to the public and to banks. To **reduce** the supply of money, it **sells** securities: the buyers pay with cheques drawn on their banks, the banks' cash reserves fall, and so they can lend less. To **increase** the supply of money, it **buys** securities and pays the sellers, so bank reserves rise and credit expands.

2. **Bank rate (discount rate or policy rate).** This is the rate at which the Central Bank lends to commercial banks. A **higher** bank rate makes borrowing from the Central Bank dearer, so that commercial banks raise their own lending rates, borrowing falls and the money supply contracts. A **lower** rate has the opposite effect.

3. **Reserve requirements (cash ratio) and special deposits.** Commercial banks must keep a given percentage of their deposits as reserves with the Central Bank. **Raising** the ratio reduces the amount that banks can lend and so reduces the money supply; **lowering** it allows them to create more credit. Special deposits freeze part of the banks' reserves in the same way.

4. **Credit ceilings and selective credit controls (directives).** The Central Bank may instruct banks to limit total lending, or to lend more to priority sectors such as agriculture and less to consumption, and to reduce or increase loans for particular purposes.

5. **Moral suasion.** The Central Bank advises and appeals to the commercial banks to restrain or to expand lending in the national interest, without any legal force.

6. **Foreign exchange operations.** By buying or selling foreign currency, the Central Bank changes the amount of local money in circulation.

**Limitations.** The instruments work well only if the banking system is well developed; people may keep money outside the banks, and banks may hold excess reserves, so the effect may be smaller than intended.

**Conclusion.** By using these instruments, the Central Bank controls the money supply and helps to keep prices stable and the economy growing.
